source.title: Who Pays More for Safety? Measuring the Disparate Cost of Safety Alignment across Languages
source.authors: Chanwoong Yoon; Jungsoo Park; Alan Ritter

record.tranche_reason: The study applies weight orthogonalization based on the refusal direction and reports its effects on harmful-response rates, refusal rates, and capability scores. It tests the practical removal claim with measures and settings different from the original study.
record.gate_note: The paper uses an abliterated weight-edit proxy and reports outcomes for that intervention. Table 15 reports unsafe-response rates; Table 17 reports refusal rates on over-refusal benchmarks; Table 18 reports P-MMEval capability averages. Results cited from other studies are not recorded as rows. The many language-by-benchmark Safety Cost results in Table 14 measure pairwise helpfulness preference, not the refusal or capability measures used in the rows below.
record.test_reason: Abliteration is a tool here, but the study reports its own measured effects for four released abliterated checkpoints (huihui-ai) against their aligned originals, across six languages. Table 15 gives unsafe-response rates on a multilingual jailbreak benchmark, Table 17 gives refusal rates on over-refusal benchmarks, and Tables 16 and 18 give P-MMEval capability. These results bear directly on whether released abliterated models lose refusal while keeping ability (V2, and the ablation half of V1). The setting is new: multilingual and large released models.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that non-English users bear a higher Safety Cost (utility loss from alignment), measured against abliterated counterparts. They say the cost arises from both explicit refusals and implicit informativeness loss. They validate the ablation proxy with confound maps, an ordinary-benign control and matched trained checkpoints. They treat abliteration itself as given, not as a claim under test.
record.recipe_differences: The study estimates a direction from harmful-versus-benign prompts and orthogonalizes model weights, following the cited refusal-direction approach. It evaluates ablation through multilingual unsafe-response, refusal, utility, and capability measures; it does not test activation addition.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary by model, language, and benchmark. The paper also reports length-matched Safety Cost results and notes that disparity magnitude changes after matching; the Qwen3 matched-checkpoint experiment gives a different Chinese cost pattern from its released-model ablation estimate.

fits_no_version.finding: Safety Cost: the pairwise helpfulness win rate of the abliterated over the aligned model on borderline-benign prompts is higher in most non-English languages for Qwen2.5 and Gemma-3. A matched train-from-base checkpoint pair gives a similar pattern to the ablation estimate for Qwen3.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Utility lost to safety alignment, measured against a refusal-ablated counterpart, falls unevenly across languages.

record.problems: The unaligned counterparts for the released models are abliterated proxies, and the authors acknowledge that ablation may marginally affect latent capacities. The refusal-rate evidence is restricted to selected benchmarks and languages in the extracted rows. Capability evidence includes aggregate averages, and the study does not test direction addition.
record.rows_left_out: Within the 60-row limit, Table 14's separate Safety Cost results for every model, language, and benchmark are not included. Table 17 has additional language-by-model-by-benchmark refusal-rate cells beyond the English and Vietnamese examples extracted here. Table 16's language-level benign-task scores and the ordinary-benign Safety Cost control in Table 13 are also omitted; these do not directly measure the refusal or general-capability outcomes represented in the kept rows.

untested.parts: Adding the direction to induce refusal. Per-layer or per-position activation ablation. How the direction was chosen: the third-party huihui-ai checkpoints are used as given.
Who made the edit and how: the direction's source prompts, language and layer for the huihui-ai models are not reported.

Direction vectors are not compared across languages. Ablation removes refusal in all six languages, but the language of the prompts used to build the direction is not stated, so transfer cannot be read.
Entire version. The matched-checkpoint experiment measures Safety Cost, not whether a removable direction exists.
Only Qwen3-32B is tested, and only Table 17 is labelled reasoning. Thinking mode is not stated for the Table 15 and Table 18 results.

missing.what: Per-subtask capability drops from abliteration: Gemma mhellaswag −7.5 and mifeval −5.0; Qwen3 mhellaswag −7.5; Qwen2.5 mhellaswag −3.3

Over-refusal refusal rates for Chinese, French, Arabic, Korean, Thai and Ukrainian. Llama XSTest stays at 4–9% abliterated; Gemma falls to 0–1% everywhere. Declared in rows_left_out but needed to compare models.

record.verdict_notes: The abliterated models are third-party huihui-ai releases. The study does not describe their direction-selection details beyond citing Arditi et al. The unsafe rate is judged by GPT-4.1; 'invalid' outputs are not reported separately. Changes of 1 point on 100 prompts are treated as negligible. The reader's 'reversed' and 'challenges' calls for r25–r26 are downgraded to absent and limits_scope. V6 is left untested because the language of the direction's source prompts is unstated, even though removal is uniform across six languages.

versions.untested_parts: The paper measures unsafe-response rates after ablation and capability averages, but does not add the direction to induce harmless-request refusals. It uses a weight edit, not an independently tested projection at every activation layer and position.
Refusal-rate changes are measured on the listed over-refusal benchmarks, not across all refusal types or requests.
No attack suppression of the direction or training against its ablation is evaluated.
The study does not compare a single direction with affine, cone, or multiple-direction accounts.
The study does not test whether harmfulness judgments and refusal decisions are separately represented.
It evaluates effects across languages, but does not compare direction vectors across languages, model variants, or base and instruct models.
A matched-checkpoint experiment studies a safety-training intervention, but does not test whether training choices determine the existence of a removable refusal direction.
No reasoning-model test of V1 is reported.

relation.reason: Tables 15, 17 and 18 give measured effects of the weight edit on refusal/unsafe behaviour and capability. These bear directly on V2 (and V1).

tranche.reason: Abliteration is the study's tool, but it reports its own unsafe-rate, refusal-rate and capability comparisons of released abliterated checkpoints against their parents, in a new multilingual, large-model setting. So it is not T4.

source_check.notes: The unaligned models are third-party huihui-ai checkpoints (Table 3), and the study gives no edit details beyond A.1. There is no random-direction control or uncertainty on the rates. Appendix C.2 implies the main Qwen3-32B runs used thinking mode, so the Table 15/18 Qwen3 rows (unsafe 75-79%; capability -3.7) may also bear on V8. Table 17's Avg column does not equal the mean of the four model columns. The cells were placed by column grouping.

statements.correction: Llama-3.3-70B-IT-abliterated English unsafe rate 30.48% vs aligned 7.94% (Table 15); 29.52-34.92% across six languages.
statements.problem: Correct. The measure is the unsafe-response rate (GPT-4.1 judge, multilingual jailbreak benchmark, English), not a refusal rate. The judge also has an 'invalid' class, so the remaining ~70% are not all refusals.

statements.correction: arXiv:2608.22490: no uncertainty reported on unsafe or refusal rates; capability check yes (P-MMEval). Fourth checkpoint huihui-ai Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct-abliterated: unsafe 7.94-16.19% -> 29.52-34.92% across six languages.
statements.problem: The numbers are right (baselines 3.17-10.16%, abliterated 60.00-85.40%). But 'uncertainty' is wrong for these rates: Tables 15/17/18 give no CIs or error bars, and ± appears only on translation-quality scores. The controls (ordinary-benign set, matched checkpoints) check Safety Cost, not the abliteration effect, and there is no random-direction control. The study's fourth checkpoint is left out.

statements.correction: Qwen3-32B P-MMEval avg 69.23 -> 65.52, mhellaswag 70.94 -> 63.49 (Table 18; mode not stated). n=100 prompts per benchmark per language. No CIs.
statements.problem: The four Qwen3-32B refusal numbers are right. But 'uncertainty' is not reported for them. The direction method is only described as contrastive harmful-vs-benign pairs, and the huihui-ai procedure is not given. Thinking mode is shown only by the Table 17 header 'reasoning'. 'Capability mostly kept' leaves out a moderate Qwen3 drop.
No numbers given for this study. Listing it as V1-style removal in a reasoning model is fair, but the evidence is only over-refusal (benign borderline) prompts with 3-17% baselines.
